**Prefix caching reuses intermediate computation for identical token prefixes; semantic response caching reuses an earlier answer for a similar request.** The former can preserve the model's intended computation under valid cache conditions. The latter changes the application behavior and can return an incorrect answer even when embeddings are close. [1](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/)[2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

Imagine “What is my account balance?” asked by two different customers. The requests are nearly identical in wording but require different answers. A semantic cache keyed only by text similarity would leak or confuse user-specific information. Even the same customer's answer may become stale after a transaction.

A response-cache entry therefore needs an applicability boundary: tenant and authorization context, relevant data version, model and prompt version, response policy, and freshness requirements. A similarity threshold is only one part of the decision. Requests involving mutable personal state may need exact structured keys or no response caching at all.

Prefix caching is different: when the token prefix and necessary model/cache identity match, the server can reuse previously computed key/value states and continue processing the suffix. It saves repeated prefill work, not necessarily output-token generation. Cache validity depends on implementation details such as model weights, adapters, token sequence, and isolation configuration. [1](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/)

Measure both hit rate and error rate. For a response cache, test false hits on near-neighbor requests with opposite meanings, changed dates, different permissions, and updated documents. For prefix caching, measure time to first token, memory pressure, and eviction effects under actual traffic.

**An illustrative tradeoff:** a 60% semantic hit rate looks attractive, but even a small false-hit rate may be unacceptable for account information. A lower hit rate with exact scoped keys can be better. Cache only when the system can state why reuse is valid; semantic similarity is evidence of related wording, not equivalence of the required answer. [3](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)[4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)[5](https://research.google/pubs/the-ml-test-score-a-rubric-for-ml-production-readiness-and-technical-debt-reduction/)
